findings.title: Unpinned remote script piped to sh at build time (supply chain)
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` fetches and executes remote code during the image build with no version pin, checksum, or signature. The image bytes are therefore whatever the endpoint serves at build time, fully controlled by whoever owns/compromises that domain or endpoint (or a certificate/DNS-level compromise). Anyone who builds this Dockerfile (CI, release pipeline, local `docker build`) executes that code as root inside the build, and the resulting image is non-reproducible. `-L` also lets the server redirect the fetch to an arbitrary other host.

findings.title: curl failure swallowed by pipe; build succeeds on failed install
findings.whyItBreaks: In `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh`, the RUN exit status is `sh`'s (last command of the pipeline), not curl's. `-s` suppresses the error message and no `-f`/`--fail` (and no `pipefail`) is set, so when the download fails before/while producing a body (DNS failure, connection refused, empty body), `sh` receives empty input and exits 0 — the build reports success while the install step never ran. The downstream layers at Dockerfile:4 (`COPY app /app`) and Dockerfile:5 (`CMD ["/app"]`) then bake a runtime image that silently lacks whatever the script installs, and external build orchestration cannot distinguish this from success. With the base Dockerfile there was no such step, so this silent-failure path is newly introduced.

findings.title: Run no longer blocks, so results are delivered after it returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, Run blocked on each `results <- j * 2` (old line 7) and returned only after every job result had been sent, in job order. Now each send runs in a detached goroutine, so Run returns immediately and the sends happen after the call returns and in nondeterministic order. Any caller that follows the prior contract and closes `results` once Run returns (e.g. `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)`) races those goroutines and panics with `send on closed channel`; a caller that reads/aggregates `results` after Run returns observes an incomplete or empty set. Run is exported, so this contract change applies to every caller; no in-repo caller exists to cite, but the changed lines themselves are the defect.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord OR-guard allows cross-tenant and non-admin record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaces `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` with `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. With OR, the predicate now returns true in two cases that it previously rejected: (1) any non-admin session whose tenantId matches the record's tenantId (previously required isAdmin), and (2) any admin session regardless of tenantId (previously required tenant match). Since this function is the sole authorization guard for a destructive delete operation and it is exported as the public boundary (`canDeleteRecord`, src/permissions.ts:12), both loosened branches are authorization bypasses: a same-tenant non-admin gains the ability to delete arbitrary records (including other users' records — `RecordRef.ownerId` is not consulted), and an admin gains the ability to delete records belonging to other tenants, breaking tenant isolation. There are no call-sites in this repo (edges = []) so nothing downstream re-validates the decision; the exported function's contract is itself the boundary, so the weakening ships as-is.

findings.title: Swallowed parse/validation failure causes updateFontSize to overwrite stored settings with DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (swallowed failure). Before this change, parseSettings threw on invalid JSON, non-string theme, or non-number fontSize (base: `if (typeof data.theme !== "string") throw new Error("bad theme")` / `if (typeof data.fontSize !== "number") throw new Error("bad fontSize")`), and that throw propagated out of updateFontSize at line 20, aborting BEFORE `save(JSON.stringify(settings))` at line 22 — so a corrupt store was left untouched. The new `catch { return { ...DEFAULTS }; }` at lines 14-16 converts that failure into a legitimate-looking value, so updateFontSize proceeds: it reads the fallback `{theme:"light", fontSize:14}`, overwrites fontSize with `size` (line 21), and persists line 22. Failure is no longer distinguishable from success at the consumer. Concretely, stored `{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"}` (or a partial `{"theme":"dark"}` / malformed JSON) yields a saved `{"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}`, permanently losing the user's theme and any other field rather than surfacing an error. parseSettings is exported, so external callers that relied on the throwing contract are likewise forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: pageCount() floors, dropping the trailing partial page
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount is the exported public contract for 'how many pages totalItems items occupy at pageSize per page'. The body now returns Math.floor(totalItems/pageSize) (src/pagination.ts:3). For any non-divisible total this undercounts by one page: pageCount(10,3) returns 3 (base ceiled to 4), pageCount(1,10) returns 0 (base 1). A caller that iterates pages 0..pageCount-1 then renders/serves items 0..(pageCount*pageSize-1) and silently drops the final partial page — item index 9 in the (10,3) case and the sole item in the (1,10) case. The unchanged carrier (name pageCount, signature pageCount(totalItems, pageSize): number @src/pagination.ts:1) still promises a page count, so the change makes promise != implementation. No in-repo caller exists (rg found only the definition); the defect ships at the module boundary, so any external consumer paginating by this count loses data.

facts.meaning: The page count rounds down instead of up.

findings.title: Report lists artifacts from "verified" but builtFrom records branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported carrier BuildReport.builtFrom (src/report.ts:7) is documented by name as the commit the report's artifacts were built from, and the prior body honored that by passing the same `commit` to both fields. The changed body (src/report.ts:13-14) sets builtFrom = build.ref(branch) while pulling artifacts from build.ref("verified"), a different ref. Any caller comparing builtFrom to the artifact source, or reconstructing provenance, now sees two different commits in one report; for a branch whose tip differs from "verified" the listed artifacts did not come from builtFrom. No in-repo consumer exists to trace (rg found none), but the mismatch is on the exported public contract itself, which affects the data a caller receives.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores `limit`, making renderFeed return unbounded pages
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc carrier on line 1 promises 'Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first', but the body now returns the entire reversed array for any limit > 0 (src/feed.ts:5), so the promise is not implemented. The only in-repo caller, renderFeed, relies on that promise: it allocates `new Array<string>(20)` (src/feed.ts:10) and copies `page.length` items (src/feed.ts:11). Before the change `page.length === min(20, all.length)`, so the loop only filled the pre-allocated 20 slots; now `page.length === all.length`, and `out[i] = page[i]` for i >= 20 extends the array (JS array growth on out-of-range index assignment), so renderFeed(all) with >20 items returns all entries instead of at most 20. This is a behavior regression for any caller feeding more than 20 values (unbounded result size / dropped cap).

findings.title: entry-count header counts stale entries not emitted as rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `live = entries.filter((e) => !e.stale)` (line 20) drops stale entries from `rows` (line 21), but the unchanged header still receives `entries.length` (line 22), so `# entry-count` equals the full input list including stale entries while the manifest body emits only live rows. When any entry has `stale === true`, the header declares more entries than there are rows, so any consumer reconciling the declared count against the rows (pre-sizing to entry-count, asserting row count == entry-count, or reading `entry-count` rows after the two header lines) mis-parses or rejects a well-formed manifest. Verified by substitution: input `[{path:'a',stale:false},{path:'b',stale:true}]` emits rows `a` only (1 row) but header `# entry-count: 2`.

findings.title: execute() now always throws, replacing working uppercase transform
findings.whyItBreaks: The body changed from `return input.toUpperCase()` to `throw new Error("always fails")`. `execute` is the repo's only export (nothing else references it in-repo, verified via rg), so the exported behavior is the public contract: callers that previously received a transformed string now always get an exception on a path that has no failure precondition. This is not a tightened guard on a legitimately-approvable action (the old code had no failing branch); it is an unconditional, value-independent failure for all inputs. The signature at src/runner.ts:1 still annotates `): string`, but the body can never return, so the public contract is broken (TypeScript does not catch this because a never-returning body is assignable to any return type).

findings.title: Viewer guard in isEligible blocks the legitimate read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible now returns false for any viewer (src/handler.ts:18). handle gates all routing on it at src/handler.ts:24 (`if (!isEligible(req)) return "rejected";`), so the viewer-specific branch at src/handler.ts:25 (`if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";`) is now unreachable. Substituting real values: an active viewer with attempts=0 was previously handled as "read-only"; it now returns "rejected". Viewers were eligible before this change (old isEligible only checked status and MAX_ATTEMPTS), and line 25 exists precisely to serve them, so this changed predicate rejects an action that is legitimately approvable on its own.

findings.title: Payment gate leaks into saveDraft, blocking unpaid draft saves
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared gate read by two distinct actions. saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9) uses `if (!canProceed(order)) return "blocked"`, but saving a draft does not and should not require payment: a draft by definition has payment === "missing". With the new predicate `order.state !== "ready" && order.payment === "paid"`, a normal draft order (state "draft", payment "missing") now fails canProceed, so saveDraft returns "blocked" instead of "saved". The added condition legitimately governs submission (submitOrder, src/actions.ts:4) but not draft-saving, so it rejects an action that is approvable on its own. Previously `canProceed` was only `state !== "ready"`, so unpaid drafts saved fine.

findings.title: publishSnapshot returns files from a different commit than it reports
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change files came from repo.filesAt(head), where head = repo.headCommit(channel) (line 13), so Snapshot.commit and Snapshot.files described the same tree. Now line 14 fetches a second, unrelated ref ('stable') and line 18 builds files from it, while line 16 still sets commit to the channel's head. Any consumer of the exported Snapshot (interface field files at line 9, contract on stdout via commit at line 16) receives a commit id paired with a file list taken from a different commit; verifying files against snapshot.commit or publishing the set at the reported commit yields wrong/missing data. rg confirms no in-repo caller yet, but publishSnapshot/Snapshot are exported, so the mismatch is the shipped API contract.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positive validation its body does not enforce
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff renames read_int -> parse_positive_int (line 1), but the body is unchanged: `return int(value)` (line 2) accepts any int-parsable string, so parse_positive_int('-5') == -5 and parse_positive_int('0') == 0. It is an exported module-level carrier whose name now promises a positivity contract (validated/positive) that the implementation does not implement. The in-repo consumer charge() relies on that promise at src/validators.py:6 (`n = parse_positive_int(amount)`) and turns it into a billing amount at src/validators.py:7 (`return n * 100`), so negative/zero inputs yield negative cents which total_cents() (src/validators.py:10-11) then sums. A caller trusting the name skips its own validation and gets a passed-through negative value instead of a rejection.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates caller DataFrame in place instead of returning a copy
findings.whyItBreaks: BASE returned a new object (`result = df.copy()` then `return result`) leaving the argument untouched; HEAD assigns onto the caller's own frame (`df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` @src/transform.py:6) and returns that same aliased object (@src/transform.py:7). Any caller that keeps the reference it passed in, or that uses the returned value and the original interchangeably, now observes its input rewritten — e.g. a caller reading the pre-call `"value"` column after invoking apply_values gets the rewritten values, corrupting previously-held state. The previous per-call defensive copy was the only thing guaranteeing the input's immutability, and it was dropped. No in-repo caller exists (`rg apply_values` matches only the definition), so the blast radius is external consumers of this exported module-level function, whose contract changed without any signature/doc change to signal it.

findings.title: Workflow relocated out of .github/workflows disables all CI
findings.whyItBreaks: The only workflow file was renamed from .github/workflows/ci.yml to docs/ci.md with 100% identical content. GitHub Actions only discovers workflow definitions under .github/workflows/*.yml|yaml, so at HEAD no workflow is registered: the `on: push` / `on: pull_request` trigger (docs/ci.md:2-4) and its lint+test job (docs/ci.md:10-12) never run, and any status check that gated merges vanishes. README.md:5 still promises 'CI runs lint and tests on every push.' (Note: even at BASE the job referenced npm ci/lint/test with no package.json present, so the check was likely already red; the regression is that the trigger/gate itself is now gone, not that a green gate was lost.)

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves items, breaking items.len() and the build
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!($val)` expands to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, so `items` is moved by value into the macro at src/store.rs:2. The value returned by the macro is then discarded by the trailing semicolon. The unchanged statement `let total = items.len();` at src/store.rs:3 consequently reads `items` after the move, which is a compile error (E0382: use of moved value) — `process` cannot build at all. `dbg!` additionally unconditionally formats and writes its argument to stderr on every call, so even if it compiled it would inject stray debug output into this public function's side-effect profile.

findings.title: changeset base revision diverges from revision the diff was computed against
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported contract at src/changeset.ts:7-9 states fromRevision is "Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision." The change at line 15 introduces `latest = store.resolve("latest")` and line 18 computes `changedPaths` from `latest`, but line 17 still returns `fromRevision: from` = `store.resolve(pinnedTag)` (line 14). So the diff base (latest) and the reported base (pinnedTag) are two different revisions. A consumer that replays `changedPaths` onto `fromRevision` (the documented usage, and the only way to use the returned pair) applies a diff computed against the wrong revision — either applying changes that do not belong on the pinned revision or missing the intended changes, silently producing a wrong replay result. The two fields must name the same revision; when pinnedTag != latest they never can here.

findings.title: Column rename orphans SELECT email consumer
findings.whyItBreaks: The migration executes `ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN email TO contact_email`, so after it runs the `users` table has no `email` column. The sole consumer src/query.sql:1 does `SELECT email FROM users;`, which now fails (column does not exist). Nothing in the surface updates the consumer to the new name, so any query path using src/query.sql errors after migration 0002 is applied.

findings.title: Non-concurrent index build blocks writes to users table
findings.whyItBreaks: `CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email)` at migrations/0002_index.sql:1 is built without CONCURRENTLY. On the populated table defined at migrations/0001_init.sql:1, Postgres takes a SHARE lock on `users` for the whole scan/sort/build, which conflicts with ROW EXCLUSIVE; every concurrent INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (signup, login, profile writes) blocks until the build completes and the transaction commits. Against live traffic this stalls or times out user writes for the build duration, proportional to table size.

findings.title: Live-looking billing API key hardcoded in source
findings.whyItBreaks: The credential source changed from process.env.BILLING_API_KEY to a source literal "bk_live_9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0". The value is now committed to git, visible to everyone with repo access, impossible to rotate without a code change, and shared across all deployments/environments. Any out-of-repo caller of makeClient() that receives the returned BillingClient.key will transmit this fixed key as a production credential.

findings.title: Removed fail-fast guard silently masks unconfigured credential
findings.whyItBreaks: Trigger D (swallowed failure): the base version threw Error("BILLING_API_KEY is not set") at src/billing/client.ts:7 (base) when the key was absent, so misconfiguration surfaced at startup. The change deletes that propagation; makeClient() now always returns a value, so a caller can no longer distinguish 'credential missing' from 'credential present'. makeClient is an exported/public function, so the API contract itself is the defect: every eventual caller is forced to treat a misconfigured/revoked-credential state as a legitimate key, and the failure is deferred to a later, harder-to-diagnose billing call.

findings.title: Inverted admin gate lets non-admins delete archived projects
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code deleted only when `user.isAdmin && project.archived`. The rewrite makes the admin check reject the authorized case (`if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden";`) and simply falls through for non-admins. Trace a non-admin against the new guard: user.isAdmin=false → line 12 not taken; project.archived=true → line 13 not taken; line 14 executes `db.delete(project.id)` and line 15 returns "purged". So a non-admin caller reaches the destructive db.delete (line 14), an authorization bypass on a data-persistence path.

findings.title: Admin purge permanently blocked by inverted guard (over-block)
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER A over-block: the gated action is 'admin purges an archived project' (db.delete at src/projects.ts:14). The changed predicate at line 12 now returns "forbidden" whenever user.isAdmin is true, so an admin can never reach the delete — the action that was legitimately approvable under the base contract (admin && archived → purged) is unconditionally rejected. Distinct from the bypass in the other finding: here the legitimate authorized action is denied.

facts.meaning: The refactored guard incorrectly returns forbidden for administrators.
Non-administrators can reach the destructive project purge/delete path.

findings.title: startup() crashes on missing config after None-fallback removed
findings.whyItBreaks: startup() still consumes load_settings()'s contract: load_settings returns None when the settings path does not exist (app/config.py:7). The deleted guard previously converted that None into {"workers": 1, "region": "us-east-1"}, so startup(path) succeeded and returned 1 for an absent config. After the change, the None flows straight into the dereference at app/config.py:14 (`settings["workers"]`), which raises TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable. Any caller invoking startup() against a not-yet-created config file — the exact case the removed fallback existed for — now fails instead of getting the default worker count/region.

findings.title: Charge returns nil on gateway failure, masking failed charges as success
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` with `log.Printf("charge failed: %v", err)` (pay/charge.go:17) and falls through to `return nil` (pay/charge.go:19). The exported signature `func Charge(...) error` (pay/charge.go:12) promises an error on failure; the body now returns nil on every `gw.Submit` error, so callers that branch on the returned error (e.g. `if err := pay.Charge(...); err != nil { ... }`) cannot distinguish a failed charge from a successful one. This is a money-movement entry point: an out-of-repo caller will treat a declined/failed charge as paid and may mark the order paid, ship goods, or bill the customer. No in-repo caller exists (rg for `Charge` matches only its definition), so the affected consumer is the out-of-repo API caller relying on the documented error return.

findings.title: Tenant-agnostic cache key returns one tenant's settings to another
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) (src/settings.ts:8) returns `settings:${name}` with no tenantId, and settingsFor now derives its cache key from it (src/settings.ts:12). The first tenant to populate a given `name` writes that key (src/settings.ts:16); every subsequent tenant that asks for the same `name` hits the guard `if (hit !== undefined) return hit;` (src/settings.ts:14) and is returned the other tenant's stored value, skipping store.fetch(tenantId, name) (src/settings.ts:15). This is a cross-tenant data disclosure plus stale-value bug on a live read path.

findings.title: invalidate() dropped tenantId, breaking existing two-arg callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature changed from invalidate(tenantId, name) to invalidate(name). A JavaScript caller still invoking invalidate(tenantId, name) binds name=tenantId and deletes `settings:${tenantId}` (src/settings.ts:21), so the intended entry `settings:name` is never invalidated (stale reads persist) and an unrelated setting whose name equals the tenantId is deleted. TypeScript consumers get a hard arg-count error; JS consumers silently misbehave. The export is a public contract, so the blast radius is every external caller, not just in-repo ones.

findings.title: reserve() race: await between check and decrement oversells stock
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, reserve() was synchronous, so the read of this.stock (line 15), the guard `if (remaining <= 0) return false` (line 16), and the write `this.stock.set(sku, remaining - 1)` (line 18) ran without yielding and could not interleave. The new `await this.store.save(sku, remaining - 1)` (line 17) yields the microtask queue before line 18 commits the decrement, so two concurrent reserve() calls for the same sku both read `remaining = 1`, both pass the line-16 guard (which no longer sees the other call's yet-uncommitted decrement), both persist and set stock to 0, and both return true — two reservations granted for one unit (oversell/lost update). Substitution on real values: caller A reads 1 -> passes line 16 -> suspends at line 17; caller B reads 1 -> passes line 16 -> suspends at line 17; both write save(sku,0) and set(sku,0). The guard at line 16 no longer rejects the stale value it was written to reject.

findings.title: backoff() unit change double-scales retry() delays ~1000x
findings.whyItBreaks: src/config/backoff.ts:2 changed the returned unit from seconds (Math.min(30, 2**attempt)) to milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt*1000)). The unchanged consumer src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still calls `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, and `sleep` (src/jobs/retry.ts:3) already treats its argument as ms, so the new ms value is multiplied by 1000 again. Substituting real values: attempt 0 -> backoff=1000 -> sleep(1_000_000 ms) = 1000 s (~16.7 min, was 1 s); attempt >=5 -> backoff=30_000 -> sleep(30_000_000 ms) = 30_000 s (~8.3 h, was 30 s). Both consumers of the exported symbol were affected; only src/net/poll.ts:4 was updated, so retry() now effectively hangs for hours.

findings.title: Save discards Close error, returning nil on failed persist (data loss)
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Save's success/failure was decided by `return f.Close()` (base a182d6d:24) and the flush+close sequence (base:20-24) propagated any Close error to the caller. Now the file is closed via `defer f.Close()` at store/save.go:13 whose error is thrown away, and the only returned error is `w.Flush()` at store/save.go:20. bufio.Flush() only guarantees the buffered bytes were handed to the OS via write(2); it does not guarantee durability. On filesystems where errors are surfaced at close (NFS/CIFS, delayed-allocation/ENOSPC/EIO/EDQUOT), Close can fail after a successful Flush, so Save returns nil even though the lines were never persisted. This is the canonical Go doc warning ("the error returned by Close on a file opened for writing") and it silently converts a persist failure into a success — the exact failure-as-value conflation this data-write primitive is the sole guard against. As the only exported persistence primitive (and with no in-repo callers), the exported error contract itself is the defect: every eventual caller is forced to treat a failed write as success.

findings.title: page_window drops the last row of every page (range end-1)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a correct exclusive end (end = min(start+page_size, row_count), line 20), but the collection loop was changed from range(start, end) to range(start, end - 1), so it stops one element short and never appends rows[end-1]. Every page silently loses its final row. Substituting rows=['a','b','c','d','e'], page_size=2: page_window(page_index=0) -> start=0, end=2, range(0,1) -> ['a'] (base returned ['a','b']); page_index=1 -> ['c'] (drops 'd'); page_index=2 -> range(4,4) -> [] (drops 'e', and emits an empty page). The consumer render_page (lib/pagination.py:40) then renders only the truncated window, and summarize (lib/pagination.py:52) joins those truncated pages, so the displayed/exported line set loses one row per page and the final page can render as an empty string with a trailing separator.

findings.title: TtlCache.get inverts TTL check: serves expired, evicts fresh
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate was < (return value while age < ttlMs, i.e. still fresh) and is now > (return value only while age > ttlMs, i.e. already expired). Substituting a real entry stored 5s ago with ttlMs=60000: age=5000, 5000 > 60000 is false, so the branch falls through to this.entries.delete(key) at src/cache.ts:21 and get() returns null — a fresh, legitimate cache hit is rejected and destroyed. Conversely for an entry stored 120s ago (age=120000 > 60000 true), get() returns entry.value at src/cache.ts:19 — an expired value is served as valid. This gates the 'may the caller receive the cached value' decision for the public get() contract; it both rejects the legitimately-returnable fresh value and approves the un-returnable expired one. TRIGGER A: call-sites enumerated — the predicate is read only at src/cache.ts:18 inside get(); rg found no in-repo consumers of TtlCache (only src/queue.ts, unrelated), so the distinct gated action ('return cached value to caller') exists solely for external callers; the change makes it reject the approvable fresh state. TRIGGER C: carrier name TtlCache/public get() promises freshness-only returns; body at src/cache.ts:18-22 implements the inverse, and the promise affects the value every caller receives.

findings.title: pruneDone skips consecutive done jobs via splice-during-forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: The loop calls jobs.splice(index, 1) at src/queue.ts:9 while forEach (src/queue.ts:7) is iterating the same array. Each removal shifts later elements left by one, but forEach advances to index+1 anyway, so the element that moved into the removed slot is never visited. For jobs=[{done:true},{done:true}] the first iteration splices index 0 leaving [{done:true}]; forEach has no index 1 and stops, so the function returns an array that still contains a done job. The previous filter implementation correctly removed all done jobs. Any caller that trusts the result to contain only not-done jobs (e.g. re-dispatching the returned queue) will re-process finished work.

findings.title: pruneDone mutates and returns the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation (return jobs.filter(...)) produced a new array and left the input untouched. The new body splices the passed-in array at src/queue.ts:9 and returns the same reference at src/queue.ts:12, so any caller that still holds the original `jobs` reference observes its done entries silently disappearing. This is an observable regression of the exported function's prior non-mutating behavior; no in-repo consumer exists, so the affected party is external callers holding the original reference.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty input instead of 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` was deleted. For an empty array `rows.reduce((sum, row) => sum + row.amount, 0)` yields 0 and `rows.length` is 0, so `total / rows.length` evaluates to `0 / 0` = NaN. Any consumer that sums, averages, or compares this result now propagates NaN (and every NaN comparison is false), whereas the previous exported contract returned 0. The repo has no in-repo callers, so the failing path is the exported function itself; blast radius is external importers of this public API.

findings.title: busiest sorts and mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous body copied first (`const ranked = [...rows].sort(...)`); it is now `rows.sort((a, b) => b.amount - a.amount)[0]`. Array.prototype.sort sorts in place and returns the same reference, so calling the exported query `busiest(rows)` destructively reorders the caller's array as a side effect. A caller that keeps using its array after calling busiest (or shares it) observes reordered data, unlike before.

findings.title: Lexicographic sort corrupts leaderboard cutoff and ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() with no comparator coerces numbers to strings and compares UTF-16 code units, so ordering is lexicographic, not numeric ('100' < '20' < '3'). rankScores returns this wrong order and topPlayers derives cutoff from it at src/leaderboard.ts:15 and filters with `p.score >= cutoff` at src/leaderboard.ts:16: for players [{score:5},{score:40}], n=1, rankScores yields [5,40] (['40']<['5'] reversed), cutoff=5, filter keeps both and slice(0,1) returns the score-5 player, so the true top player (40) is dropped. Negative scores are similarly mis-ordered ('-5' sorts after '3' lexicographically). formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:20) renders this wrong result directly.

findings.title: verify() uses non-constant-time `==`, reintroducing a timing oracle on the signature
findings.whyItBreaks: BASE compared the expected digest against the caller-supplied signature with `hmac.compare_digest`, which is constant-time; HEAD replaces it with `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature`. Python's str `==` short-circuits at the first differing character, so comparison time varies with the number of matching leading hex characters. An attacker who can measure response timing for chosen `given_signature` values can recover the expected digest one nibble at a time and then submit the recovered value, defeating the check that gates processor(payload). The consuming decision is handle() @app/webhook.py:14 (`if not verify(...)` -> 401 vs 200+processor(payload)); the boolean is still functionally correct, but the comparison is no longer constant-time, which is the security property the auth predicate must preserve.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the ledger transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base, the ledger INSERT, the debit UPDATE, and the credit UPDATE all ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block (base app/transfer.py:4-16), so any failure rolled back all three together. Now only `_record_ledger` is inside the transaction (app/transfer.py:22-23) and `_apply_balances(db, from_acct, to_acct, cents)` is invoked after the `with` block exits (app/transfer.py:24). Once the transaction block at app/transfer.py:22 commits, the ledger INSERT is durable; a subsequent failure or crash in `_apply_balances` (either UPDATE in app/transfer.py:9-16) leaves a committed ledger row with no debit/credit applied. Because the two UPDATEs at app/transfer.py:9-12 and app/transfer.py:13-16 are no longer wrapped by this transaction, they are also not atomic with each other: a fault between them debits one account without crediting the other, creating/destroying money. `transfer` raising does not roll back the already-committed ledger row, so callers cannot distinguish a completed transfer from a partially-applied one.

findings.title: billingDay now buckets by host-local day, not UTC (TZ/DST dependent)
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 4 is the only behavior change in the hunk: the body now reads at.getFullYear()/getMonth()/getDate() (local) where it previously read getUTCFullYear()/getUTCMonth()/getUTCDate() (UTC); the extracted pad helper is behavior-preserving. The exported billingDay therefore now returns a value that depends on the runtime's ambient timezone (process.env.TZ / host config) and on DST, so the same instant yields different billing days on different hosts, and timestamps near local midnight shift to the previous/next day versus the old UTC bucketing. Because there is no timezone parameter, 'local' is the server's zone, not any business/user zone, so the result is non-deterministic across deployments. sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8) reads billingDay directly and inherits the new semantics: two instants that were distinct UTC days can now compare equal (and vice versa), mis-grouping charges by day. Example: billingDay(new Date('2026-09-27T00:30:00Z')) = '2026-09-27' under TZ=UTC but '2026-09-26' under TZ=America/New_York.

findings.title: Memo keyed by account alone leaks profiles across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account`, so the module-level `memo` no longer partitions entries by tenant. On line 15 `memo.get(key)` is the sole guard before the `fetchProfile` short-circuit on line 16, and line 18 `memo.set(key, profile)` writes under the same tenant-unaware key. If tenant A and tenant B share an account string, a readProfile(tenantB, ...) call hits the entry written by tenant A's fetchProfile and returns A's Profile (with A's displayName/tenant) without ever calling fetchProfile — a cross-tenant data-disclosure/correctness bug. readProfile is exported, so the blast radius extends to all consumers.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error, returns "" that callers can't distinguish from real value
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch-all wrapper (src/store.ts:6-7) discards the `Error(`missing: ${key}`)` failure signal raised at src/store.ts:4 and returns "" instead. load() is exported, and its only in-repo caller loadAll() at src/store.ts:12 maps every requested key through load(), so a missing key now contributes an empty-string entry rather than propagating an error. Callers of loadAll() receive a string[] that is not shorter and not flagged — the value "" is indistinguishable from a key that was legitimately stored with an empty-string value, and the `missing: <key>` diagnostic (which key failed) is destroyed. The catch also swallows any unexpected error from store.get (e.g. a throwing/custom Map), with no logging, so failure and fallback are conflated at every decision point.

findings.title: Exported rename timeoutMs→timeout breaks importers and silently disables the deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported; changing `timeoutMs: number` to `timeout: number` (line 4) is a breaking API change — typed importers that pass {timeoutMs} no longer compile, and untyped/JS importers keep sending timeoutMs while the body now reads config.timeout (line 8 in retry, line 21 in retryBackground). With config.timeout undefined, `deadline = Date.now() + undefined` is NaN, and the guard `Date.now() > deadline` (line 10 / line 23) is always false, so the timeout is silently disabled and the loop runs every attempt regardless of elapsed time. The rename also drops the millisecond unit the old name promised, while the body still computes Date.now()+ms. A second required field, retries (line 3), is added but ignored by retry(), so existing retry() callers must also supply a value it never uses.

findings.title: New exported retryBackground swallows every failure and returns void
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground catches every error from fn and `continue`s (lines 27-29); when all attempts fail, or when the deadline exits early (line 23), it returns void (line 20) with no signal. Callers cannot distinguish total failure from success, so a background job that never succeeded is indistinguishable from one that did — the exact conflation Trigger D forbids for an exported swallow site. previously_reached: not applicable for the new function; the analogous swallow in the pre-existing retry (lines 14-16) is unchanged and out of surface.

findings.title: Widened `value: string | number` unimplemented: `value.length` is undefined for numbers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported carrier `FieldProps.value` (line 2) was widened to `string | number`, promising numbers are valid inputs, but the body reads `value.length` (line 6). For a `number`, `.length` is `undefined`, so `label` becomes the literal `len=undefined` and the `<input defaultValue={label}>` (line 7) renders that wrong text; the value the caller supplied is never used. TypeScript also rejects `.length` on the union `string | number`, so the module as written does not type-check. Substituting the newly-allowed value number 42: `label = "len=" + (42).length = "len=undefined"`.

findings.title: Echoing repo secret TOKEN into workflow logs exposes credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 11 binds the repository secret `secrets.TOKEN` to the step env var `TOKEN`, and line 12 (`run: echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`) interpolates that value directly into stdout, so the credential is written to workflow logs that the job produces `on: push`. GitHub's log masking is best-effort (registered exact values only; it does not survive any transformation/encoding or any secret value the runner fails to register), so the only thing preventing plaintext credential disclosure here is masking rather than the workflow. Any collaborator or log reader with repo read access, and the entire public if the repo is public, is the exposure surface.

findings.title: git() lost its 64 MiB maxBuffer; >1 MiB diffs now abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: git() now calls spawnSync with no maxBuffer, so it falls back to Node's default of 1024*1024 bytes (verified: `spawnSync('bash',['-c','<2MB stdout>'],{encoding:'utf8'})` returns status=null and error.code='ENOBUFS', not status=0). When `git(['diff', mergeBase, headSha])` at src/adapters/github.ts:140 emits more than ~1 MiB, the guard at src/adapters/github.ts:38 (`res.status !== 0`) sees null !== 0 and throws. That call is outside the try/catch that starts at line 176, so runGithub aborts and NO GitHub check-run is posted for any PR whose diff exceeds ~1 MiB (previously handled up to 64 MiB). The same applies to the changed-file diff at src/adapters/github.ts:57 (changedFileSet, invoked at line 141), whose output can also exceed 1 MiB on many-file PRs. The thrown message is also empty because stderr is empty on ENOBUFS, making the failure opaque.

findings.title: Dropping `-s read-only` unstages the only write brake on headless codex
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns headless `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 24) and prompt on stdin; `codex exec` is non-interactive, so the sandbox mode is the only thing preventing the child from writing files or running mutating commands in the review target. The removed CLI flag `-s read-only` is what pinned that sandbox, and CLI flags outrank `~/.codex/config.toml`. After this change the sandbox value falls through to ambient config/defaults. Concrete substitution verified on this host: `~/.codex/config.toml` sets `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` and `approval_policy = "never"`, so the previously-overridden value now wins and the child runs with full filesystem/network access and no approval gate. A prompt, or hostile content in the reviewed repo, can then delete/overwrite files in `opts.repoPath` (data loss) or execute arbitrary commands, and the process can exfiltrate repo contents. The wrapper's other control (returning only last-message text) does not prevent filesystem mutation. Even where config sets a less permissive mode, the confinement is no longer deterministic across machines.

findings.title: Review patch/file-set drift to base-branch commits (merge-base dropped)
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code isolated the PR's own commits via `git diff merge-base(baseSha,headSha) headSha`. New line 139 runs a two-dot `git diff baseSha HEAD` against the raw base SHA (`PR_BASE_SHA` / GitHub `base.sha`, the base-branch tip), and line 140 feeds the same raw `baseSha` to `changedFileSet` (which diffs `--name-only baseSha HEAD`, github.ts:57). When the base branch advanced after the PR forked, commits merged into base are now included in `bundle.patch` and appear reversed (base-only content rendered as deletions), and those base-only paths are added to `changedPaths`. Consumers: `review(bundle)` at src/adapters/github.ts:176 reviews the wrong diff text, and `changedPaths.has(f.file)` at src/adapters/github.ts:63 then admits findings whose files are not in the PR, so inline comments can target non-PR files/lines (GitHub's reviews API rejects those; the catch at github.ts:96 reposts and silently drops ALL inline comments).

findings.title: Patch diffed against HEAD while PR_HEAD_SHA (headSha) annotates the review
findings.whyItBreaks: `headSha` (github.ts:137) deliberately honors `PR_HEAD_SHA`, and old code diffed against that value. New line 139 diffs against the literal `HEAD` (`changedFileSet` does too, github.ts:57). When `PR_HEAD_SHA` is set and the checked-out HEAD differs — e.g. Actions checks out `refs/pull/N/merge`, so HEAD is the merge commit while PR_HEAD_SHA is the PR head — `bundle.patch`/`changedFiles` describe HEAD's tree, yet the review is posted against a different commit (`commit_id: headSha` at src/adapters/github.ts:85 and `head_sha: headSha` at src/adapters/github.ts:124). Inline comment line numbers come from the HEAD-based patch but are anchored to the headSha commit, so GitHub rejects them and the github.ts:96 fallback reposts the review with zero inline comments.

findings.title: Plain-string replace mangles $&/$`/$' in bundle/findings/patch prompt text
findings.whyItBreaks: Lines 25, 32 and 33 pass the payload directly as String.replace's replacement (line 25 JSON.stringify(bundle,...), line 32 JSON.stringify(candidate,...), line 33 bundle.patch). When the replacement is a string (not a function), JS interprets $$ $& $` $' $n $<name> inside it; the base revision used () => value so the payload was emitted verbatim. bundle.bundle.patch / JSON.stringify(bundle) and the model's candidate JSON are arbitrary diff/user text that routinely contains '$'. Substitution proof: patch text 'const re = /a$&b/' becomes 'const re = /a{{PATCH}}b/'; a bash ANSI-C quote "$'...'" in the patch expands to the entire critic.md text after {{PATCH}}, and "$`" expands to all text before {{PATCH}} (which already includes the substituted findings JSON), duplicating prompt content and dropping the literal diff. Consuming locations: runCodex(criticPrompt) at src/core/review.ts:34 and runCodex(reviewPrompt) at src/core/review.ts:28 then review a corrupted/duplicated bundle/patch, producing wrong findings and verdict.

findings.title: Fallback review loses commit_id pinning to reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary payload still pins the review via `commit_id: headSha` (src/adapters/github.ts:89), but the catch-fallback POST at the reviews endpoint (src/adapters/github.ts:101-112) no longer sends `commit_id`; the hunk deleted `commit_id=${headSha}` between `event=` and `body=` (HEAD lines 108-110). GitHub's create-review API documents `commit_id` as defaulting to the most recent commit in the PR when omitted, so when the fallback fires (the `--input -` JSON POST throwing) the review is anchored to the PR's latest commit rather than `headSha`. Concurrently the same run posts a check-run explicitly pinned to `headSha` (`head_sha: headSha`, src/adapters/github.ts:128 via postCheck call at line 184), so the resulting state is inconsistent: the check evaluates/seals the reviewed SHA while the fallback review (COMMENT/REQUEST_CHANGES) attaches to a different commit, and a re-review of a non-latest SHA or a push that lands between job start and posting is mis-anchored. The original hunk's companion inline comments are absent in the fallback, which bounds (but does not eliminate) the impact.

findings.title: Malformed findings are coerced into fabricated findings instead of rejected
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously threw on any invalid severity/category/file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix/line (base schema.ts:96-122) and normalizeReview's non-strict path caught and DROPPED such findings (base schema.ts:158-165). The new body maps every failure to a default value: invalid severity -> 'P1' (line 98), invalid category -> 'bug' (100-102), missing title -> 'Untitled finding' (99), missing file -> '' (103), missing/invalid lines -> 0 or NaN via Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0) with the Number.isFinite/'>0' guards removed (104-105), empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix (107-108). normalizeReview now always maps through this coercer and its strict/drop propagation branch is gone (line 131). Concrete substitution: normalizeFinding({}) returns {severity:'P1', title:'Untitled finding', category:'bug', file:'', lineStart:0, lineEnd:0, whyItBreaks:'', suggestedFix:''} instead of throwing, and normalizeReview(raw) never drops it. Downstream callers therefore cannot distinguish 'model emitted a malformed finding' from 'model emitted a real P1 bug', and the synthesized finding (empty file, 0 lines, P1 severity) is reported/billed as a real result. This is an exported/public API, so the contract defect ships regardless of in-repo callers (no in-repo consumer exists: the repo contains only this file).

findings.title: Removing `-R "$REPO"` breaks PR ref resolution before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: These `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` calls lost `-R "$REPO"` (REPO: ${{ github.repository }} was also deleted at line 30), yet the `refs` step runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (line 42). `gh` can only infer the target repo from a git remote in the CWD (or GH_REPO); at this point the workspace is not a checkout, so no remote exists. The previous code pinned the repo deterministically to github.repository; now gh either errors ('not a git repository / could not determine base repo') or infers a stale/foreign remote left on the self-hosted runner. Because each call is `echo "head=$(...)"`, the failure is discarded as an empty value: `head=`/`base=` are written to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and under `bash -e` a failed command substitution inside `echo` does not fail the step, so this is silent. At the consumer `actions/checkout` (`.github/workflows/review.yml:45`) `ref: ''` falls back to the triggering/default-branch ref rather than the PR head, and `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (`.github/workflows/review.yml:56-57`) are passed empty to `src/cli.ts --github`, so the review is computed against the wrong commit while still being posted to the PR.

findings.title: Loose candidate parse silently drops findings instead of failing
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview's second parameter is `strict` (default true). With strict=false it wraps normalizeFinding in try/catch and filters out any finding that fails validation (invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, lineEnd<lineStart, or a P0-P2 finding with confidence<0.7) instead of throwing. So at line 29 a malformed candidate finding is silently mapped to `absent`, not reported. The only guard the pipeline runs is line 30 (`!candidate.summary || candidate.checked.length === 0`), which reads fields unaffected by the flag, so it passes even when findings were dropped. The candidate (now incomplete) is serialized into the critic prompt at line 35 as if it were the complete first-pass result, and the returned review takes `findings: pruned.findings` at line 48 from a critic that only prunes the candidate list it is handed. Net effect: a genuinely-detected finding whose JSON has a minor schema defect is discarded and the review can return a partial verdict (potentially pass) with no signal that anything was lost. Previously the same input threw loudly instead of yielding a misleading partial review.

findings.title: normalizeReview now silently swallows malformed output as an empty valid review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the five throw branches that previously propagated malformed model output (old schema.ts:115-131: non-object, non-string summary, non-array findings/checked/residual_risks) and replaces them with `Array.isArray(...) ? ... : []` and `String(raw?.summary ?? "")`. Every failure signal is now mapped to a default value, so a null, a truncated JSON payload such as `{"summary":"..."}` that parsed without findings/checked/residual_risks, or a wrong-type field all yield the SAME object as a legitimately empty review: `{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}`. normalizeReview is an exported symbol returning a value type (RawReview), so callers have no error channel; their previous try/catch and error paths are now dead and they cannot distinguish 'model output was malformed/truncated' from 'reviewer found nothing'. In a review pipeline this propagates downstream as a successful zero-finding review (default verdict pass). No in-repo consumer exists (repo has only this file; hotspot edges[] is empty), so the defect is the exported API contract itself, per the Trigger D exported-swallow rule — every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Manual dispatch reviews empty range: PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA now sourced only from pull_request context
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are read straight from github.event.pull_request.base.sha / head.sha. On workflow_dispatch there is no pull_request payload, so both expressions evaluate to empty. The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step existed exactly for this case: its else-branch ran `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid/baseRefOid` (base lines 39-43) and fed non-empty shas into these env vars and into the checkout ref. The workflow still advertises the trigger (`on.workflow_dispatch.inputs.pr_number`, description 'manual trigger; bypasses pull_request webhook', line 13) and still runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts --github --pr <n>` at line 47. Downstream (consumer src/cli.ts, an external checkout artifact — line unresolved per the hotspot edge; the CLI resolves its base..head range from these env vars, e.g. `PR_HEAD_SHA || ...` / `PR_BASE_SHA || ...` with a `Could not resolve PR base/head SHA` guard), an empty head/base no longer selects PR #N's range: at the matching tool revision the CLI falls back to `git rev-parse HEAD` and `git merge-base origin/main HEAD`, so with the dispatch checkout also falling back to github.ref (line 29) HEAD == origin/main and diff(range) is empty ('No diff ... Nothing to review') or the resolve guard throws. Either way the manual-trigger action no longer reviews the requested PR's diff. This is the same state commit 094a271e2b fixed by introducing the Resolve step; this diff reverts that fix.

findings.title: git() maxBuffer removal breaks capture of large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line drops the explicit `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` so `spawnSync("git", ...)` falls back to Node's documented default maxBuffer of 1024 * 1024 (1 MiB). Git output is capped per stream and the child is terminated when exceeded; on this Node line that sets `res.error` (ENOBUFS) and leaves `res.status` null, so the unchanged guard `if (res.status !== 0)` at line 12 evaluates true and the caller throws `git diff <base> HEAD failed: ` with empty stderr, aborting the whole review. Even in the variant where the process exits 0 first, stdout is truncated, so the patch bound at line 100 (`const patch = git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)`) is silently incomplete and the non-empty check at line 106 cannot detect it, feeding `review(bundle)` a partial patch. The sibling helper `gh()` still sets `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` at line 36, so this is an unintended asymmetry: previously any diff up to 64 MiB was captured, now any diff over ~1 MiB (routine for large PRs/vendored/generated files) fails or loses data. Also affects line 101 `git(["diff", "--name-only", baseSha, "HEAD"])` whose truncated output flows into `classifyFiles()` at line 102, changing the changed-file/surface list.

findings.title: Errored review now reports neutral check, unblocking required check
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path now posts conclusion "neutral" (src/adapters/github.ts:191) even though the same check's summary still asserts "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR." (src/adapters/github.ts:193) and the process still sets a non-zero exit (src/adapters/github.ts:196). That conclusion string is written verbatim into the check-runs request body's `conclusion` field (src/adapters/github.ts:126, posted via the call at src/adapters/github.ts:187), which is exactly what branch protection / required status checks read; `neutral` (already used for the legitimate needs_human verdict, src/adapters/github.ts:53) is treated as passing for required checks. So a run in which `review()` throws — no review produced at all — now reports a mergeable conclusion, and callers can no longer distinguish "review failed to run" from the legitimate "needs_human" neutral state. The previous `failure` value blocked the merge.

findings.title: Review workflow now runs PR-authored tool/install scripts with write token
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff deletes the trusted-tool checkout (base lines 51-56) and runs both the install and the review against the untrusted PR-head checkout in the default workspace. Line 51 `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` executes PR-authored lifecycle scripts (postinstall/prepare) from the PR's package.json, and line 59 `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` executes the PR's own review tool. Both run with GH_TOKEN (line 56) which is granted `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` (lines 18-19) on a `self-hosted` runner (line 23). The job `if:` (line 24) only excludes fork heads, so any same-repo branch author (or a workflow_dispatch run, whose description explicitly bypasses the webhook) can rewrite the reviewer to post a passing review/check-run for its own PR, exfiltrate the token, or persist code on the reused self-hosted runner. Base ran the tool from `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/needlefish` (base line 70), so PR content never executed with the token; the removed comment at base lines 3-6 documented exactly this guarantee, which this change removes.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Dropped severity coercion misclassifies valid lowercase/padded severities
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code coerced with `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before the allow-list check; the change compares the raw value directly via `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)`. Substituting raw.severity='p1' (or ' P2 ', both legitimately valid severities modulo casing/whitespace) now yields false and falls to the default, so a real P1/P2 is silently reclassified. The function's whole purpose (name `normalizeFinding`, exported carrier) is to normalize such input, and its only in-repo consumer normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:132) feeds raw external findings straight through it, so the mis-normalization propagates into RawReview.findings.

findings.title: Unknown/malformed severity silently downgraded to P3 (fail-open default)
findings.whyItBreaks: The fallback for a severity that fails the allow-list changed from 'P1' to 'P3'. Substituting any unrecognized value (undefined, '', 'critical', or the now-rejected 'p1') returns P3, the least-severe classification, instead of the previous conservative P1. normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:132) passes this value through unmodified into RawReview.findings with no distinguishing marker, so a downstream severity-gated consumer (triage/ordering/verdict thresholds, out-of-repo) cannot tell a malformed finding from a genuine P3 and will under-prioritize or filter it — the opposite of the prior fail-closed behavior.

findings.title: Codex subprocess re-inherits GitHub token env after scrub removal
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deleted the `const env = { ...process.env }` copy plus `delete env.GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN` and removed the `env` option from this spawnSync call. `spawnSync` defaults its `env` option to `process.env` when omitted (Node docs: options.env Default: process.env), so at src/shared/codex.ts:23-29 the codex `exec` child — a model-driven agent process receiving an arbitrary prompt — now receives GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN that the base revision at a48217a specifically stripped. The previously-withheld credentials are exposed to the LLM-controlled subprocess, a trust-boundary regression at the process-execution edge. `runCodex` is an exported entry point (no in-repo callers), so the defect ships as the API contract and every external caller is affected.

findings.title: Fork PRs now run untrusted code on self-hosted runner with repo token
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` from the `review` job (base line 19), leaving no fork filter anywhere in `.github/workflows/` (rg for `head.repo.full_name` now returns nothing). The workflow is still triggered by `pull_request: [opened, synchronize, reopened]` (line 8) on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18). A fork PR therefore reaches each downstream consumer: checkout of untrusted `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (line 23), `corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` executing the fork's dependency lifecycle/scripts under `zsh -l` (line 28), and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` running the fork-controlled tool with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (line 33). Permission block (lines 11-14) requests `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`, and `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` is the automatic token; even under GitHub's fork read-only downgrade, arbitrary fork code still executes on trusted self-hosted infrastructure, enabling persistent host compromise and lateral access to whatever credentials/caches the runner holds. The token is only one of the exposed assets.

findings.title: Explicit 0 duration silently replaced by fallback, delaying SIGKILL escalation
findings.whyItBreaks: Changed predicate `parsed > 0` rejects the previously-supported value 0 (base used `parsed >= 0`). Substitute the real value: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 -> trimmed="0", Number("0")=0, Number.isFinite(0)=true but 0>0 is false, so line 135 returns fallbackMs=5000 instead of 0. That value initializes RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS (@3) and is consumed at @124 as the delay between SIGTERM and SIGKILL, so an operator asking for no grace / immediate SIGKILL now gets a 5s uninterruptible wait. The same substitution for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 yields 2000 instead of 0, consumed at @123 as the give-up timer after SIGKILL, adding a further 2s before finish(). 0 is a legitimate setTimeout delay (immediate) and was explicitly accepted by the old `>= 0` guard; the new guard therefore rejects a legitimately-approvable value and silently overrides an explicit operator setting.

findings.title: Uncovered changed files silently skipped in large-PR deep review
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed backstop (old lines 97-110) was the only code that appended a tail hotspot for changed files absent from the risk-sorted hotspots. Findings are produced only by the loop over `hotspots` (line 97) and merged at line 108, and `hotspots` is truncated to `MAX_HOTSPOTS`=6 at line 93. Any changed file not assigned to one of those 6 surfaces is therefore never deep-reviewed and its defects cannot reach the critic, even though its diff is in the PR; the deleted code guaranteed coverage via `bundle.changedFiles` minus `covered`.

findings.title: Single deep-pass error now aborts the entire large-PR review
findings.whyItBreaks: The try/catch that wrapped each per-hotspot deep pass was removed, so any error from `runCodex`/`extractJson`/`normalizeReview` at line 103 propagates out of `reviewLarge` and rejects `review()` at line 135 — the exact path taken for large PRs. Previously the failure was converted to a `{blocks:true}` residual risk and the remaining hotspots still ran; now one transient deep-pass failure yields no findings, summary, or verdict at all. Line 113 also forces `residual_risks: []`, so deep-pass residual risks no longer reach the critic's candidate input (the critic's own `pruned.residual_risks` is still what line 128 returns).

findings.title: Deep prompt no longer substitutes {{FOCUS}}, leaking literal token
findings.whyItBreaks: The deep prompt chain now only replaces {{AGENTS}}, {{HOTSPOT}}, {{BASE}}, {{HEAD}}. The removed line (base 122, `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")`) was the sole substitution of {{FOCUS}} in the codebase (rg over the surface finds zero remaining `FOCUS` references). The template prompts/deep.md:96 still contains `Focus: {{FOCUS}} (if not "(none)", prioritize findings in that area)`, so every per-hotspot deep pass now feeds the model the raw mustache placeholder instead of the user's focus (or "(none)"), and a caller-supplied focus is silently ignored. Base code substituting the token is direct evidence the placeholder was part of the contract.

findings.title: mapBundle drops `focus`, so map.md cannot rank surfaces by focus
findings.whyItBreaks: mapBundle now serializes only baseSha/headSha/patchStat/changedFiles/agentsMd. prompts/map.md:37 instructs `If a \`focus\` field is set (not null), rank matching surfaces higher`, but the field is no longer present in the JSON handed to the map pass, so the condition can never be true and focus-prioritization is lost for every large PR. reviewSmall (line 54) still JSON.stringifies the whole bundle including focus/deep, so the two review paths now diverge.

findings.title: formatDuration can emit "60s" / "1m 60s" after split-rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: seconds is Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000). Since ms % 60000 is in [0, 59999], the quotient is in [0, 59.999] and rounds up to 60 at the top of the range. Nothing carries that into minutes, so ms=119500 -> minutes=1, seconds=60 -> "1m 60s", and ms=59999 -> minutes=0, seconds=60 -> "60s". The old code rounded total seconds first, so ms=59999 produced "1m 0s" and ms=119500 produced "2m 0s"; both new outputs are malformed regressions that every consumer of the rendered report sees via the stats line at src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, breaking its positivity contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported helper is named `parsePositiveInteger` and its failure text (src/shared/runner.ts:33) promises it `requires a positive integer`, but the guard now only rejects `parsed < 0`. Substituting 0: `Number("0") === 0`, `Number.isInteger(0) === true`, and `0 < 0 === false`, so the guard falls through and returns 0 at src/shared/runner.ts:35. Number coercion also makes empty/whitespace input succeed: `Number("") === 0` and `Number(" ") === 0`, so a missing/blank count/limit/timeout option is silently accepted as 0 rather than rejected. Because this is an exported public boundary validator, the promise (positivity + throw on non-positive) IS the contract; 0 is not a distinguishable failure value, so any caller using the result for a count, limit, retry budget, or timeout (e.g. timeoutMs=0 = no/immediate timeout) receives an invalid value where it previously got an exception.
